sections.title: Identification
sections.text: Wild Flammulina velutipes produces smooth orange-yellow to reddish-brown caps, usually 2–7 cm but sometimes reaching 10 cm. They start convex, flatten with age and become conspicuously sticky or slimy after rain. Broad, fairly well-spaced gills are white to cream when young and pale yellow later; the spore print is white. The tough narrow stem is yellowish at the top, darkens through brown to nearly black towards the base and develops a characteristic velvety surface. There is no ring. Wild fruitbodies look quite different from the long pale forms grown commercially in low light, and the name enoki has also been applied to related cultivated Flammulina species.

sections.title: Habitat and season
sections.text: Velvet shank grows in clusters on dead or declining broadleaf trees, stumps and fallen branches, including elm, poplar, alder and willow. It is especially conspicuous in cold weather: in western Europe fruiting often extends from late autumn through winter into early spring. A winter date is a useful clue, but it cannot itself establish the species.

sections.title: Dangerous lookalikes
sections.text: Galerina marginata, the deadly funeral bell, is another brown-capped mushroom of woody habitats and may occur during mild winters. It has rusty-brown rather than white spore prints and often has a ring, though the ring may disappear with age. Kuehneromyces mutabilis also has brown spores, darker gills and a ring or ring remnants. Stem texture, gills and spore print should be assessed together; a missing ring, cap colour or season alone cannot prove safety. Check each fruitbody in a mixed cluster.

sections.title: Edibility and caution
sections.text: The German Mycological Society, Swiss VAPKO list and Woodland Trust describe velvet shank as edible when properly identified, but the Missouri Department of Conservation specifically advises against collecting wild specimens for food because of confusion with deadly G. marginata. This guide follows that cautious recommendation for wild collections. An illustration is not a food identification. If a suspected velvet shank has been eaten and identification is uncertain, contact a poison centre or medical service promptly, even before symptoms.

traits: Smooth sticky orange-yellow to reddish-brown cap, usually 2–7 cm, flatter when old
Broad spaced white-to-cream gills becoming pale yellow; white spore print
Tough stem yellowish above and dark brown to black, velvety below; no ring
Clusters on dead or declining broadleaf wood
Fruits in cold weather from late autumn into early spring
safetyNote: Wild collection for food is not recommended here. Deadly Galerina marginata can also grow in brown-capped clusters on wood, including in mild winters. A white spore print and dark velvet stem are useful identification features, but a photo or one feature cannot establish safety; seek urgent poison-centre or medical advice after uncertain ingestion.
